name: Herodotus
description: Historian from Halicarnassus. Book 4 of the Histories places the silphium country among the peoples of Libya.
image_file: Marble bust of Herodotos MET DT11742 (cropped).jpg
image_description: Roman copy of a Greek bust, second century CE
image_credit: Metropolitan Museum of Art · CC0

name: Hippocratic corpus
description: A collection of medical treatises by multiple authors. Diseases IV discusses attempts to cultivate Libyan silphium in Ionia and the Peloponnese.
image_description: Later engraving of Hippocrates, the corpus’s traditional namesake; the author of Diseases IV is unknown
image_credit: Unidentified engraver · public domain

name: Theophrastus
description: Greek philosopher and naturalist. Enquiry into Plants records the form, harvesting, range, and reported cultivation of silphium.
image_description: Modern statue at Palermo Botanical Garden
image_credit: tato grasso / Singinglemon · CC BY-SA 2.5

name: Plautus
description: Roman comic playwright. In Rudens, a character invokes a hoped-for silphium harvest and a shipment to Capua.
image_credit: Pierre François Barrois · public domain

name: Catullus
description: Roman poet of the late Republic. Poem 7 uses silphium-bearing Cyrene as a point of comparison.
image_credit: Schorle · CC BY-SA 3.0

name: Strabo
description: Greek geographer from Amaseia. Geography 17 describes a long, narrow silphium-producing region south of Cyrenaica.
image_description: Imagined portrait engraved by André Thévet in 1584
image_credit: André Thévet · public domain

name: Pliny the Elder
description: Roman encyclopedist. Two passages in Natural History discuss scarcity of Cyrenaic silphium, imported resin, and medicinal uses.
image_file: Grande Illustrazione del Lombardo Veneto Vol 3 Plinio Secondo 300dpi.jpg
image_credit: Geoffrey · public domain

name: Dioscorides
description: Greek physician and pharmacological author. De materia medica 3.80 compares silphium and resin from Libya and eastern regions.
image_description: Dioscorides depicted in the Vienna Dioscurides manuscript, c. 512 CE
image_credit: Unknown artist · public domain

name: Synesius of Cyrene
description: Writer and later bishop in Cyrenaica. Two letters mention a garden plant called silphium and a gift of its juice.
image_description: Imagined portrait engraved for André Thévet’s 1584 collection
image_credit: British Museum / André Thévet · public domain

name: Martin Martin
description: Traveller from Skye who visited St Kilda in 1697. His 1698 book describes the Gairfowl’s body, egg, and seasonal presence.
image_credit: Atlas of Historically Lost Species · original asset

name: Thomas Pennant
description: Welsh naturalist whose British Zoology describes the great auk and draws on Martin Martin’s earlier account of St Kilda.
image_description: Engraved portrait of Thomas Pennant, eighteenth century
image_credit: National Library of Wales · public domain

name: George Cartwright
description: Trader and journal writer in Labrador and Newfoundland. His entry for 5 July 1785 describes great auk harvesting at Funk Island.
image_credit: Wikimedia Commons · public domain

name: Alfred Newton
description: British ornithologist who published John Wolley’s research and interviews about the great auk in Iceland.
image_credit: The Graphic / Historian 1875 · public domain / CC0

name: Frederic A. Lucas
description: American zoologist who visited Funk Island in 1887 and mapped the great auk’s former breeding ground from terrain and surviving remains.
image_credit: Atlas of Historically Lost Species · original asset

name: Carolus Clusius
description: Author of Exoticorum libri decem (1605), which includes a description of a dodo leg in the collection of Pieter Pauw at Leiden.
image_credit: Atlas of Historically Lost Species · original asset

name: Thomas Herbert
description: Author of A relation of some yeares travaile (1634), including a description and illustration of the dodo.
image_credit: Atlas of Historically Lost Species · original asset

name: Hamon L’Estrange
description: His annotations on Thomas Browne describe a captive bird shown in London about 1638.
image_credit: Atlas of Historically Lost Species · original asset

name: François Cauche
description: His Relation du voyage appears in Relations veritables et curieuses (1651), compiled by Claude-Barthélemy Morisot.
image_credit: Atlas of Historically Lost Species · original asset

name: John Barrow
description: Travelled in southern Africa while serving under Lord Macartney at the Cape. His account includes a reported reappearance of blue antelope near Sweet Milk Valley.
image_credit: Atlas of Historically Lost Species · original asset

name: John Tyssen
description: Lieutenant commanding HMS Sparrow. Recorded the statements of Henry Whiteman and Samuel Profit after rescuing them on West Falkland in February 1842.
image_credit: Atlas of Historically Lost Species · original asset

name: Falkland Islands Magazine contributors
description: The magazine’s editor and the correspondents E. J. Smith, Thomas H. Butler and an anonymous writer signing “A Witness.” The letters concern remembered killings at Fox Bay.
image_credit: Atlas of Historically Lost Species · original asset

name: Georg Wilhelm Steller
field: Natural history · Bering’s second Kamchatka expedition
description: German physician and naturalist in Russian service. Shipwrecked with Bering’s crew on Bering Island in 1741–1742, where he described the sea cow from living and dissected animals.
image_credit: Atlas of Historically Lost Species · original asset

name: Martin Sauer
description: English secretary to Joseph Billings’s Russian expedition to north-eastern Siberia and the Aleutian Islands, 1785–1794. His published account reports the sea cow’s extinction at second hand.
image_credit: Atlas of Historically Lost Species · original asset

name: A. E. Nordenskiöld
description: Finnish-born Swedish geologist and explorer. Led the Vega expedition through the Northeast Passage, 1878–1880, and gathered testimony about the sea cow on Bering Island in 1879.
image_credit: Atlas of Historically Lost Species · original asset
